query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The phase stability of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the competition between the formation of face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC) phases, which is influenced by the alloy's composition, particularly the ratio of Co to Ni, and the resulting difference in Gibbs free energies between the two phases.

generation.intervention: Variation of Co to Ni ratio and temperature
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of FCC and BCC phases
generation.mechanism: Competition between FCC and BCC phases, influenced by composition and Gibbs free energy difference
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness with optimal Co to Ni ratio
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys with equal atomic ratios of elements
generation.boundary: Limitations in understanding of phase stability and lack of control over composition and processing conditions
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in predicting the exact optimal Co to Ni ratio and processing conditions for desired properties

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of Co to Ni ratio and temperature, with characterization of phase stability and mechanical properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted improvement in high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness is not observed with optimal Co to Ni ratio, the hypothesis is falsified, with a threshold of 10% deviation from predicted values.

cited_evidence.text: Recent developments of high-entropy alloys with high strength and high ductility draw attention to the metastability-engineering strategy. Using first-principle theory, here we demonstrate that reducing the Ta level in the refractory TiZrHfTax system destabilizes the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase and leads to the appearance of the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase embedded in the bcc matrix. The alloying-induced features of the elastic parameters for the cubic and hexagonal structures are mapped out in details, and strong sensitivity to the crystal lattice and chemistry is revealed. Results show softening of the bcc matrix with decreasing Ta concentration which ensures ductile behavior. However, the elastically nearly isotropic hcp precipitates possess enhanced resistance against shear which promotes strengthening of the TiZrHfTax dual-phase system. The present atomic-level insight provides strong evidence to the experimental observation, and emphasizes the significance of quantum-design for advanced multi-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent strength-ductility combinations.

The above results reveal that our design approach based on the difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases (ΔGbcc-fcc) can realize the fcc to bcc transformation in MEA research areas. The fraction of bcc and consequent transformation rate according to the Co content and temperature also well correspond to the thermodynamic phase stability. In this section, we discuss the microstructural evolution and phase stability, varied with the balance of Co and Ni, and their contributions to the mechanical response in detail.
